1: Dimensionality reduction. P C A, L D A, t S N E and U MAP, and V I F. Lectures twenty seven and twenty eight, with Doctor Shital Bhatt.
2: Today's roadmap. Lecture twenty seven is about fewer, cleaner features: multicollinearity and V I F, the idea of P C A, variance explained, and interpreting components. Lecture twenty eight is about labels and pictures: L D A, the classification view; t S N E and U MAP, pictures only; and which method when. The data is Wine Quality: six thousand four hundred ninety seven wines, one thousand five ninety nine red and four thousand eight ninety eight white, with eleven lab measurements.
3: Multicollinearity is when one feature can be predicted from the others. The density of wine depends on its sugar and its alcohol, so density adds almost no new information. In regression, linked features make the weights unstable and hard to read. A correlation heat map only checks pairs. The variance inflation factor, V I F equals one over one minus R squared, checks each feature against all the others, where R squared is how well the other features predict this one.
4: V I F on the wine data. Density has a V I F of fifteen point nine, residual sugar seven point two, fixed acidity four point nine, alcohol four point eight, total sulfur dioxide two point nine, pH two point eight, free sulfur dioxide two point five, and volatile acidity two. The guide: one means no link, one to five moderate and usually fine, five to ten high so check it, and above ten serious. Drop density and the largest V I F falls to two point eight four. Or use P C A, whose components always have V I F equal to one.
5: P C A, principal component analysis, finds the best new axes by rotating the data. PC one is the direction in which the data spreads the most. PC two is the next biggest spread, at ninety degrees to PC one. Then keep a few, because the first few principal components hold most of the information. Each principal component is a weighted mix of all features, the components are uncorrelated, and P C A does not use the target.
6: Always scale before P C A. P C A chases the biggest variance. Unscaled, total sulfur dioxide, with a standard deviation of fifty seven, beats density, with a standard deviation of point zero zero three. So PC one explains ninety five percent just because of units. Standard scaler gives every column a standard deviation of one. After scaling, the variance explained is twenty seven point five percent for PC one, twenty two point seven for PC two, and fourteen point one for PC three.
7: Variance explained: how many components? The scree plot shows bars for the percentage explained by each component, and a line for the cumulative percentage. Three rules. The elbow of the scree plot says keep three. The Kaiser rule, eigenvalue greater than one, says keep three. Reaching ninety percent of the variance needs seven. PC one plus PC two is fifty percent of the information in eleven features.
8: Interpreting components with loadings. A loading is the weight of a feature in a principal component. Read the largest positive and negative weights. PC one has positive weights for sulfur dioxide and sugar, and negative for volatile acidity and chlorides, so we name it a white style versus red style axis. PC two has positive weight on density and negative on alcohol, heavy versus light. PC three has positive weights on citric acid and fixed acidity and negative on pH, so acidity.
9: Check the name: P C A never saw the wine type. Red wines sit on the left, with an average PC one of minus two point five. White wines sit on the right, with an average of plus point eight. So PC one really is a red versus white style axis, even though P C A never saw the type column.
10: Reading a biplot, three rules. Features pointing in the same direction rise together, like the two sulfur dioxides. Features pointing in opposite directions mean one rises while the other falls, like density versus alcohol. And points lie towards the features they are high in.
11: Lecture twenty eight: L D A, t S N E and U MAP. Using labels to separate classes, and drawing pictures of clusters.
12: L D A reduces dimensions to separate classes. Compare with P C A. Does it use class labels? P C A no, L D A yes. What directions does it find? P C A finds directions of largest spread, L D A finds directions of best class separation. Maximum components: P C A the number of features, L D A the number of classes minus one. Main use: P C A to compress and explain, L D A to classify. For example, wine quality grouped as low, three to five, medium, six, and high, seven to nine, gives three classes, so L D A gives two components.
13: L D A beats P C A at classification. Test accuracy for the quality group: two L D A components give fifty seven point seven percent. Two P C A components give forty eight point six percent. Always guessing medium gives forty three point six percent. Same two dimensions, but L D A chose them to separate the classes.
14: t S N E and U MAP are for pictures only. For two thousand wines, red and white, they keep neighbours close, giving clear clusters. But the axes have no meaning, gaps and sizes are not reliable, the picture changes with the random seed and settings, and t S N E cannot place new rows.
15: Which method when? To find and fix linked features, use V I F, then drop or use P C A. To compress features and keep the meaning, use P C A with loadings. To separate known classes or classify, use L D A. To look at clusters in a picture, use t S N E or U MAP. And to feed a model, use P C A or L D A, never t S N E.
16: Key takeaways. V I F above ten is serious multicollinearity, density scored fifteen point nine. For P C A, scale first, and PC one plus PC two hold fifty percent of the eleven features. Name each principal component from its largest loadings. And L D A uses labels, while t S N E and U MAP are for pictures only.
